# 4.1 - Scatterplots and Lines of Best Fit {.unnumbered}

Ten students recorded how many hours they studied and their test score.

![](/images/Unit_4/4.1_study.svg){width="420px" fig-align="center"}

Each dot is one student. The students who studied more mostly scored higher. In this lesson, you describe patterns like this and draw a line to make predictions.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I describe the direction, form, and strength of a scatterplot.
- [ ] I choose a good line of best fit.
- [ ] I write the equation of a line of best fit.
- [ ] I make predictions and know when not to trust them.
:::

### 4.1.1 - Describing a Scatterplot

A {{< glink scatterplot >}} shows two numbers for each person or thing. The first number ($x$) goes across. The second number ($y$) goes up.

| | Ask | The study data |
|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | As $x$ goes up, does $y$ go up (positive) or down (negative)? No pattern at all is **no association**. | Positive |
| **Form** | Do the dots follow a line (linear) or a curve? | Linear |
| **Strength** | Are the dots close to a line (strong), loosely around it (moderate), or spread out (weak)? | Strong |
| **Unusual** | Any outliers or clusters? | None |

***

### 4.1.2 - The Line of Best Fit

A {{< glink "line of best fit" >}} follows the trend of the dots.

- It goes through the middle of the dots.
- About the same number of dots are above it as below it.

![](/images/Unit_4/4.1_study_line.svg){width="420px" fig-align="center"}

**Finding its equation.** Pick two points **on the line**. They do not have to be dots: $(2, 64)$ and $(6, 84)$.

$$
m = \frac{84 - 64}{6 - 2} = \frac{20}{4} = 5
$$

$$
64 = 5(2) + b \quad \Rightarrow \quad b = 54
$$

$$
\hat{y} = 5x + 54
$$

:::{.remember title="y-hat"}
$\hat{y}$ is read "y-hat." The hat means **predicted**. The line predicts $y$. It does not give the exact $y$ for every student.
:::

***

### 4.1.3 - Predicting

A student studies 5 hours:

$$
\hat{y} = 5(5) + 54 = 79
$$

The predicted score is **79**.

:::{.gotcha title="Extrapolation"}
Predicting far outside the data is called {{< glink extrapolation >}}. It is risky.

12 hours gives $\hat{y} = 5(12) + 54 = 114$. A test score cannot be more than 100. The data only goes from 1 to 8 hours.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Use $\hat{y} = 5x + 54$. Predict the score for 7 hours of study."}
$\hat{y} = 5(7) + 54 = 35 + 54 = 89$
:::

   ![](/images/Unit_4/4.1_car.svg){width="440px"}
